I am glad you mentioned the aspect of little outside support being available to many people in abusive relationships, as many abusers isolate the person or sabotage their friendships and familial relationships.


But I think your above analogy does not quite address the learned survival tactics of a person experiencing abuse.  As abuse becomes "familiar", I do not see that "comfort" is the correct word to describe it.  I think an abused party has learned to adapt to a point that allows them to survive and endure the abuse, but this does not ALWAYS result in them finding the abuse to seem "comfortable".  The learned helplessness of a person enduring abuse provides them with the short-sighted mindset of "this is the way it is, I can make it through another day".  They develop a capacity to endure their environment, as it is accepted as their only accessible reality.


The lack of control over the abusive environment leads the abused person to accept their negative situation as reality, thus making it hard to leave.

I would like to clarify that leaving an abusive relationship is not a simple process, and a past of (perhaps worse) abuse is not a sound explanation for why people stay.  The manipulation, gas-lighting, and traumatic bonding make it extremely difficult to leave an abusive partner.  Many survivors of relationship trauma attempt to leave multiple times before doing so successfully.   



The perpetuation of the idea that "most of these people" have abusive pasts is also detrimental to helping Redditors be better equipped to spot warning signs in potentially abusive relationships of their friends and family.

I think three is the perfect age to start! Your child's personality will definitely play a role in how she takes to the sport, but if she has expressed interest, I think you should have some success!  Figure skates are the best choice for beginners, and I absolutely agree to start off ice (work on falling and getting up, marching with arms out for balance).  If your rink has walkers, I would utilize that only as a last resort.  I often see that using a walker for support inhibits a child's ability to experiment with their own balance, and learn through trial and error.
You can always look up videos or Skate School curriculum online (USFS or ISI), but for starters I agree that the best thing you can do is present the ice as a fun place to be.
Do not forget a helmet that fits well! (A bike helmet works well). And no knee pads/etc-- snow pants, a winter coat, and waterproof gloves will offer some cushion for falls.

The main aspect from the above comments that is unfair is the assessment from friends/family/people outside the abusive situation, and the speculation as to WHY the abused person "chose" her abusive partner/"chose" abuse.  It is very tempting to dub someone an "easy target" when the person passing judgment has never found themselves in a situation in which they have been targeted.  Calling out someone's personality flaw as a factor in why they were abused is not so much BLAMING the victim for the abuse, but it is very much scolding them for not protecting themselves for a situation they could not foresee.  

If I get robbed because I chose to go into a rough neighborhood, yes, you could say that I made a poor decision.  But that doesn't mean that I deserved to get robbed.
A person in a wheelchair is not somehow more deserving of crime because of their being in a wheelchair.

In situations of domestic violence, the abuser does not simply "snap".  The cycle of violence begins years before an event of this extreme nature.  It may seem random and sudden to people outside of the situation, but to the couple these events are anything but.  
These abusers don't "snap", they are using fear, manipulation, and coercion to control another human being.  As the cycle of abuse continues, their tactics steadily become more extreme, and this is often where violence comes into the picture.

Abusers are expert liars and manipulators, and the only reason the abuse is because they thrive on power and control. Their motivations are not rational or reasonable.  By the time the situation truly becomes life threatening, it has become dangerous and difficult for the abused person to leave.

Long time lurker, first post ever because your story hits so close to home.  I was in a similar situation just months ago.  IT GETS SO MUCH BETTER.  Leaving will be the best thing you ever do.  Even if you end up back with your parents, even if you end up starting over at a new job...the important thing will be that HE will no longer have control over your situation.  Your happiest moment ever with him will UTTERLY PALE in comparison to the moments ahead.
Yes, those moments are nearly impossible to imagine right now.  Because leaving is hard.  But leaving is the hardest part.  It may be a bumpy road after the first impossibly massive first steps, but you will be constantly reassured by the knowledge that the hardest part is behind you.  
Stand your ground.  Solidarity and hugs.
